Code 
library(tidyverse)

orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv")
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv")
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv")

orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered") |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days)) |>
  mutate(
    delivery_status = if_else(
      delivery_days <= estimated_days,
      "On Time",
      "Late"
    )
  )

supply_chain_data <- orders_clean |>
  left_join(order_items, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  mutate(
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price
  )

This exploration examines how seller scale, delivery performance, freight cost, and product characteristics interact across the marketplace.

The goal is to identify which seller groups are supporting efficient marketplace growth and which groups may require more operational attention.

Business question: Which seller segments are helping the marketplace scale efficiently, and which ones are creating high fulfillment costs or weak operational performance?

Marketplace benchmark

Before comparing individual seller groups, I first calculated the overall marketplace performance.

Code 
overall_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

overall_performance
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  total_items average_delivery_days average_freight_cost average_freight_ratio
        <int>                 <dbl>                <dbl>                 <dbl>
1      110189                  12.0                 20.0                 0.321
# ℹ 1 more variable: on_time_rate <dbl>

The marketplace contains 110189 item rows.

Average delivery time is 12 days, average freight cost is 20, and the overall on-time delivery rate is 92.6%.

These values provide the benchmark for the comparisons that follow.

Code 
state_names <- tibble(
  seller_state = c(
    "SP", "MG", "PR", "RJ",
    "SC", "RS", "DF", "BA"
  ),
  seller_name = c(
    "São Paulo",
    "Minas Gerais",
    "Paraná",
    "Rio de Janeiro",
    "Santa Catarina",
    "Rio Grande do Sul",
    "Federal District",
    "Bahia"
  )
)

seller_state_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    average_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state")

top_8_states <- seller_state_performance |>
  head(8)

largest_state <- top_8_states |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

largest_state_share <-
  largest_state$total_items /
  overall_performance$total_items * 100

1. Scale and reliability

A seller group matters more operationally when it handles a large share of marketplace activity.

The first step is therefore to determine where marketplace volume is concentrated and whether those seller groups are also delivering reliably.

1.a Where is marketplace volume concentrated?

Code 
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = reorder(seller_name, total_items),
    y = total_items,
    fill = on_time_rate
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(on_time_rate, 1), "%")),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#8ecae6",
    high = "#023047"
  ) +
  expand_limits(
    y = max(top_8_states$total_items) * 1.12
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Marketplace activity is heavily concentrated in one seller state",
    subtitle = "Bar length shows item volume; labels show on-time delivery rate",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Number of Items",
    fill = "On-Time Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: São Paulo handles 78598 items, representing approximately 71.3% of marketplace activity.

This concentration matters because even a relatively small improvement in a high-volume seller group can affect a large number of marketplace items.

1.b Which states beat the delivery benchmark?

Volume alone does not show whether those seller groups are performing well.

I therefore compared each major seller state’s on-time delivery rate with the overall marketplace benchmark.

Code 
delivery_comparison <- top_8_states |>
  mutate(
    difference_from_average =
      on_time_rate - overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    performance_group = if_else(
      difference_from_average >= 0,
      "Above Average",
      "Below Average"
    )
  )

best_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(difference_from_average)) |>
  head(1)

weakest_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(difference_from_average) |>
  head(1)
Code 
ggplot(
  delivery_comparison,
  aes(
    x = difference_from_average,
    y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = difference_from_average,
      y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average),
      yend = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
    ),
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = performance_group),
    size = 4.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Above Average" = "#00A6A6",
      "Below Average" = "#EF476F"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Major seller states fall on both sides of the delivery benchmark",
    subtitle = "Distance from the overall marketplace on-time delivery rate",
    x = "Percentage Points Above or Below Marketplace Average",
    y = "Seller State",
    color = "Performance"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Rio Grande do Sul performs strongest relative to the marketplace benchmark, while São Paulo performs weakest among the eight largest seller states.

The business concern is therefore not simply which seller state is largest, but where large marketplace volume is combined with weaker fulfillment performance.

2. Operational pressure

Delivery reliability and freight burden should not be evaluated separately.

A seller group with strong delivery and low freight burden occupies a very different operating position from one with weaker delivery and higher shipping costs relative to product price.

Code 
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = average_freight_ratio,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = total_items,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = overall_performance$average_freight_ratio,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Some seller groups face pressure from both cost and delivery performance",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents marketplace item volume",
    x = "Average Freight-to-Price Ratio",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Seller groups below the horizontal delivery benchmark have weaker-than-average fulfillment performance.

Seller groups to the right of the vertical benchmark carry a higher-than-average freight burden.

The seller groups that combine both conditions deserve the closest operational attention, especially when they also handle substantial marketplace volume.

3. Marketplace activity over time

Seller performance should also be interpreted through time.

Periods of heavier activity may place additional pressure on the marketplace’s fulfillment network.

Code 
monthly_activity <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(purchase_year, purchase_month) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

peak_month <- monthly_activity |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

3.a When does marketplace activity peak?

Code 
ggplot(
  monthly_activity,
  aes(
    x = purchase_month,
    y = total_items,
    group = 1
  )
) +
  geom_area(
    fill = "#8ecae6",
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#023047",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#fb8500",
    size = 2.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ purchase_year) +
  labs(
    title = "Marketplace activity rises sharply as the business grows",
    subtitle = "Area shows monthly item volume while the line highlights the trend",
    x = "Purchase Month",
    y = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: The highest-volume period occurs in month 11 of 2017, with 8474 items.

The on-time delivery rate during that same period was approximately 87.1%.

This gives management a way to connect fulfillment performance with periods when the marketplace is carrying its greatest workload.

4. What drives freight cost?

A seller with higher freight costs is not automatically inefficient.

Some of the difference may be explained by the physical characteristics of the products that seller groups handle.

4.a Does product weight explain freight cost?

Code 
supply_chain_data |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#4361EE",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    color = "#F72585",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Heavier products generally cost more to ship",
    subtitle = "The highlighted trend shows the overall weight-to-freight relationship",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Freight cost generally increases as product weight increases.

This means part of the freight burden is associated with product mix rather than seller performance alone.

4.b Does that relationship change across seller states?

I then separated the four largest seller states to determine whether the same weight-to-freight pattern appears in each market.

Code 
top_4_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(4)

top_4_state_names <- top_4_states$seller_name
Code 
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_4_state_names) |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "gray70",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = seller_name),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ seller_name) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Minas Gerais" = "#F72585",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "São Paulo" = "#7209B7"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The freight relationship changes across major seller states",
    subtitle = "Each highlighted line shows the state-specific weight-to-freight pattern",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  guides(
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: All four major seller states show a positive relationship between product weight and freight cost, but the strength and shape of that relationship are not identical.

The state-specific trend lines therefore suggest that product weight explains part of freight cost, while seller location and other fulfillment factors may also contribute.

5. Freight cost variation

Average freight cost can hide substantial differences between individual shipments.

To look beyond the average, I combined a violin plot and a boxplot for the five largest seller states.

Code 
top_5_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(5)

top_5_state_names <- top_5_states$seller_name

highest_freight_state <- top_5_states |>
  arrange(desc(average_freight_cost)) |>
  head(1)
Code 
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_5_state_names) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = seller_name,
      y = freight_value,
      fill = seller_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average freight cost hides large differences between shipments",
    subtitle = "Violin shapes show the distribution while boxplots highlight center and spread",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    fill = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()

What this shows: Santa Catarina has the highest average freight cost among the five largest seller states at approximately 26.

The distributions also show that some seller states have much greater variation in freight cost than others.

This distinction matters because consistently expensive shipments represent a different operational issue from a smaller number of unusually expensive orders.

6. Management takeaway

The exploration shows that seller performance should not be evaluated using volume, delivery performance, or freight cost in isolation.

High-volume seller groups deserve attention because even small improvements can affect a large number of marketplace items.

At the same time, higher freight cost should not automatically be interpreted as seller inefficiency because heavier products naturally cost more to ship.

Management should focus most closely on seller groups that combine:

  • high marketplace volume,
  • delivery performance below the marketplace benchmark,
  • freight burden above the marketplace benchmark,
  • substantial freight-cost variation, and
  • freight costs that cannot be fully explained by heavier products.

Taken together, these measures provide a more balanced way to identify which seller groups support efficient marketplace growth and where operational improvements could have the greatest impact.

This exploration examines how seller scale, delivery performance, freight cost, and product characteristics interact across the marketplace.

The goal is to identify which seller groups are supporting efficient marketplace growth and which groups may require more operational attention.

**Business question:** Which seller segments are helping the marketplace scale efficiently, and which ones are creating high fulfillment costs or weak operational performance?

## Marketplace benchmark

Before comparing individual seller groups, I first calculated the overall marketplace performance.

```{r}
overall_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

overall_performance
```

The marketplace contains **`r overall_performance$total_items` item rows**.

Average delivery time is **`r round(overall_performance$average_delivery_days, 1)` days**, average freight cost is **`r round(overall_performance$average_freight_cost, 1)`**, and the overall on-time delivery rate is **`r round(overall_performance$on_time_rate, 1)`%**.

These values provide the benchmark for the comparisons that follow.

```{r}
state_names <- tibble(
  seller_state = c(
    "SP", "MG", "PR", "RJ",
    "SC", "RS", "DF", "BA"
  ),
  seller_name = c(
    "São Paulo",
    "Minas Gerais",
    "Paraná",
    "Rio de Janeiro",
    "Santa Catarina",
    "Rio Grande do Sul",
    "Federal District",
    "Bahia"
  )
)

seller_state_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    average_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state")

top_8_states <- seller_state_performance |>
  head(8)

largest_state <- top_8_states |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

largest_state_share <-
  largest_state$total_items /
  overall_performance$total_items * 100
```

## 1. Scale and reliability

A seller group matters more operationally when it handles a large share of marketplace activity.

The first step is therefore to determine where marketplace volume is concentrated and whether those seller groups are also delivering reliably.

### 1.a Where is marketplace volume concentrated?

```{r}
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = reorder(seller_name, total_items),
    y = total_items,
    fill = on_time_rate
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(on_time_rate, 1), "%")),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#8ecae6",
    high = "#023047"
  ) +
  expand_limits(
    y = max(top_8_states$total_items) * 1.12
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Marketplace activity is heavily concentrated in one seller state",
    subtitle = "Bar length shows item volume; labels show on-time delivery rate",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Number of Items",
    fill = "On-Time Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r largest_state$seller_name`** handles **`r largest_state$total_items` items**, representing approximately **`r round(largest_state_share, 1)`%** of marketplace activity.

This concentration matters because even a relatively small improvement in a high-volume seller group can affect a large number of marketplace items.

### 1.b Which states beat the delivery benchmark?

Volume alone does not show whether those seller groups are performing well.

I therefore compared each major seller state's on-time delivery rate with the overall marketplace benchmark.

```{r}
delivery_comparison <- top_8_states |>
  mutate(
    difference_from_average =
      on_time_rate - overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    performance_group = if_else(
      difference_from_average >= 0,
      "Above Average",
      "Below Average"
    )
  )

best_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(difference_from_average)) |>
  head(1)

weakest_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(difference_from_average) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  delivery_comparison,
  aes(
    x = difference_from_average,
    y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = difference_from_average,
      y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average),
      yend = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
    ),
    linewidth = 1,
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = performance_group),
    size = 4.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Above Average" = "#00A6A6",
      "Below Average" = "#EF476F"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Major seller states fall on both sides of the delivery benchmark",
    subtitle = "Distance from the overall marketplace on-time delivery rate",
    x = "Percentage Points Above or Below Marketplace Average",
    y = "Seller State",
    color = "Performance"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r best_delivery_state$seller_name`** performs strongest relative to the marketplace benchmark, while **`r weakest_delivery_state$seller_name`** performs weakest among the eight largest seller states.

The business concern is therefore not simply which seller state is largest, but where large marketplace volume is combined with weaker fulfillment performance.

**What this shows:** Seller groups below the horizontal delivery benchmark have weaker-than-average fulfillment performance.

Seller groups to the right of the vertical benchmark carry a higher-than-average freight burden.

The seller groups that combine both conditions deserve the closest operational attention, especially when they also handle substantial marketplace volume.

This means part of the freight burden is associated with product mix rather than seller performance alone.

### 4.b Does that relationship change across seller states?

I then separated the four largest seller states to determine whether the same weight-to-freight pattern appears in each market.

```{r}
top_4_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(4)

top_4_state_names <- top_4_states$seller_name
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_4_state_names) |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "gray70",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = seller_name),
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.7
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ seller_name) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Minas Gerais" = "#F72585",
      "Paraná" = "#F8961E",
      "Rio de Janeiro" = "#2A9D8F",
      "São Paulo" = "#7209B7"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The freight relationship changes across major seller states",
    subtitle = "Each highlighted line shows the state-specific weight-to-freight pattern",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  guides(
    color = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** All four major seller states show a positive relationship between product weight and freight cost, but the strength and shape of that relationship are not identical.

The state-specific trend lines therefore suggest that product weight explains part of freight cost, while seller location and other fulfillment factors may also contribute.

## 5. Freight cost variation

Average freight cost can hide substantial differences between individual shipments.

To look beyond the average, I combined a violin plot and a boxplot for the five largest seller states.

```{r}
top_5_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(5)

top_5_state_names <- top_5_states$seller_name

highest_freight_state <- top_5_states |>
  arrange(desc(average_freight_cost)) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_5_state_names) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = seller_name,
      y = freight_value,
      fill = seller_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average freight cost hides large differences between shipments",
    subtitle = "Violin shapes show the distribution while boxplots highlight center and spread",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    fill = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = "none"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r highest_freight_state$seller_name`** has the highest average freight cost among the five largest seller states at approximately **`r round(highest_freight_state$average_freight_cost, 1)`**.

The distributions also show that some seller states have much greater variation in freight cost than others.

This distinction matters because consistently expensive shipments represent a different operational issue from a smaller number of unusually expensive orders.

## 6. Management takeaway

The exploration shows that seller performance should not be evaluated using volume, delivery performance, or freight cost in isolation.

High-volume seller groups deserve attention because even small improvements can affect a large number of marketplace items.

At the same time, higher freight cost should not automatically be interpreted as seller inefficiency because heavier products naturally cost more to ship.

Management should focus most closely on seller groups that combine:

- high marketplace volume,
- delivery performance below the marketplace benchmark,
- freight burden above the marketplace benchmark,
- substantial freight-cost variation, and
- freight costs that cannot be fully explained by heavier products.

Taken together, these measures provide a more balanced way to identify which seller groups support efficient marketplace growth and where operational improvements could have the greatest impact.
